llm.summary: The skill's documentation describes an updater that reads local OpenClaw configs, sends notifications, and restarts the gateway, but the package contains only docs (no scripts or install spec) and does not declare required credentials or platform restrictions — the pieces don't fully line up.

dimensions.detail: The described capabilities (cron-aware updates, idle detection, risk assessment, notifications, gateway restart) are plausible for an updater. However the registry bundle contains only SKILL.md/README and no scripts or install spec. The README instructs users to run scripts/scripts/self-updater.ps1 and to install via ClawHub or git clone of a GitHub repo — none of which are present in this package. Also the SKILL.md claims Windows/PowerShell dependency but the registry entry does not enforce an OS restriction. This mismatch between claimed functionality and what the package actually includes is incoherent.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The instructions explicitly instruct running PowerShell updater scripts and reading user config files (~/.openclaw/openclaw.json and ~/.openclaw/cron/jobs.json). Reading those config files is relevant to cron-aware behavior, but those reads are not declared in requires.env and could expose tokens or sensitive configuration. The docs also mention auto-restarting the gateway and auto-detecting notification channels (Telegram/Feishu) — actions that imply service control and use of credentials, but no concrete, in-package mechanisms are provided. Because runtime behavior depends on external scripts (not included), the exact scope of what would run is unknown.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec in the registry entry and no code files. The README suggests installation via 'clawhub install' or cloning a GitHub repo, implying that the real executable code lives externally. That means to function the agent or user would need to download and run external code from GitHub/ClawHub — an additional network download step outside the registry. The lack of included scripts combined with an external-install expectation is a security and coherence concern.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill declares no required environment variables or primary credential, yet it claims to auto-detect and send notifications via Telegram/Feishu and to read ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json (which may contain API tokens). It also requires PowerShell, npm and clawhub CLI per docs, and needs permission to restart the gateway. Requesting access to local config files that likely contain credentials is proportionate for a cron-aware updater only if the package clearly documents which secrets it will use and where they come from; here those details are missing.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill is not 'always:true', and autonomous invocation is the platform default. However the updater's intended actions — restarting the gateway and performing unattended updates when AutoApprove is set — are high-privilege operations. Because the package gives no implementation and no explicit install-time consent workflow, it's unclear how restart privileges or unattended operation would be gated. Combined with the other inconsistencies, this elevates concern about unintended privilege use.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This registry entry is documentation-only: it describes PowerShell scripts and behavior but does not include the actual updater code. Before installing or running anything: 1) Do NOT run remote or local updater scripts (e.g., scripts/self-updater.ps1) until you have inspected their source from a trusted repository. 2) Verify the GitHub repo and the scripts it points to; inspect any network calls, credential usage, and restart commands. 3) Expect the updater to read ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json and ~/.openclaw/cron/jobs.json — these may contain API tokens or sensitive settings; confirm what will be read/transmitted. 4) Confirm whether your gateway restart privileges are required and acceptable; test in a staging environment first. 5) If you want notifications, ensure you understand where Telegram/Feishu tokens must be stored (and limit their scope), or prefer manual approvals. 6) If you need this functionality, prefer installing from an auditable source (official GitHub release) and only after reviewing the actual scripts. If you cannot inspect the external code, treat this skill as untrusted.
